lead: Logical equivalence is when two formulas have the same truth value in every row of a truth table. Laws of logic are named equivalences that let you replace one formula by another without changing its meaning. They turn long expressions into short ones and expose structure. The contrapositive is the one rewrite of an implication that is always safe. These ideas are used in circuit design, program verification and clear proof writing.
prereq: You need: truth tables and connectives from 1.1.

blocks.text: Two formulas are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row of their joint truth table. Write p ≡ q. The definition is exact: p ≡ q when p↔q is a tautology. A tautology is a formula that is true in every row, as covered in 1.1.
Example: ¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q. Check the four rows of p and q. Both sides are false only when p and q are both true; in the other three rows both sides are true. The two formulas match in every row.

Laws of logic are equivalences you can use as rewrite rules. The substitution principle says: if a formula A is equivalent to B, you may replace A by B inside any larger formula and the truth value does not change. Some syllabi call these laws identities.
In the table, p, q and r are any propositions. T is a tautology and F is a contradiction. The laws hold when the letters are replaced by whole formulas, not just single letters.

head: Law
Equivalence
Reads as
rows: one operator spreads over the other
not pushes inside and flips the operator
the smaller p absorbs the larger term
p or its opposite is always true; p and its opposite is always false

blocks.text: To simplify a formula, first remove → and ↔ using the implication and equivalence laws. Then apply De Morgan, distributive and absorption laws. Finish with identity, domination and negation laws. De Morgan extends to quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Quantified equivalences are treated fully in 1.6.

For the implication p→q, three related formulas are named. The converse is q→p. The inverse is ¬p→¬q. The contrapositive is ¬q→¬p. The original and the contrapositive are logically equivalent. The converse and the inverse are not equivalent to the original; they are equivalent to each other.

Look at the one false row of p→q: p true and q false. The contrapositive is false in exactly the same assignment: ¬q true and ¬p false means q false and p true. The converse is false when q true and p false, a different row. The inverse is false in that same different row, so the converse and inverse match each other.
Proof by contrapositive proves p→q by proving ¬q→¬p. This is a standard proof method; see 1.7. A common error is to prove the converse and call it the original.

figure.caption: The simplification removes the implication, factors q, kills ¬p∧p, and leaves q. Every box is logically equivalent to the one above it.

spec.title: Simplifying (p→q)∧(p∨q)
spec.aria: A five-step vertical simplification; the final box q is the simplified formula.

examples.question: Simplify ((p→q)∧(p∨q)) using laws of logic. Also write the converse and contrapositive of p→q. Verify by truth table that the simplified formula matches q.
steps: Remove the implication using p→q ≡ ¬p∨q. The formula becomes (¬p∨q)∧(p∨q).
Factor q using the distributive law: (¬p∨q)∧(p∨q) ≡ (¬p∧p)∨q.
Apply the negation law: ¬p∧p ≡ F. The formula becomes F∨q.
Apply the identity law: F∨q ≡ q. The simplified formula is q.
The converse of p→q is q→p. The contrapositive of p→q is ¬q→¬p.
Check the four rows for p and q: (T,T), (T,F), (F,T), (F,F). The original expression (p→q)∧(p∨q) is true in 2 of 4 rows, namely (T,T) and (F,T). The formula q is true in the same 2 of 4 rows.
examples.answer: The formula simplifies to q. The converse is q→p and the contrapositive is ¬q→¬p. Both the original expression (p→q)∧(p∨q) and q are true in 2 of 4 truth-table rows.
examples.check:
from itertools import product
rows = list(product([True, False], repeat=2))
def imp(a, b):
    return (not a) or b
formula_true = 0
q_true = 0
for p, q in rows:
    f = imp(p, q) and (p or q)
    if f:
        formula_true += 1
    if q:
        q_true += 1
print(formula_true)
print(q_true)
print(len(rows))

traps: Do not treat the converse q→p as equivalent to p→q. Only the contrapositive ¬q→¬p is equivalent.
Do not confuse the inverse ¬p→¬q with the original. The inverse is equivalent to the converse, not to p→q.
De Morgan: ¬(p∧q) is ¬p∨¬q, not ¬p∧¬q. The operator flips when the not moves inside.
Do not use p→q ≡ ¬p∨q and then forget the brackets. For example, ¬p∨q∧r is not the same as (¬p∨q)∧r.
Absorption only removes a term of the form p∧(p∨q) or p∨(p∧q). It does not remove unrelated terms such as p∨(q∧r).

quiz.q: Explain why p→q and q→p are not logically equivalent. Give one truth assignment that separates them.
quiz.a: Take p false and q true. Then p→q is true, but q→p is false. So the two formulas differ in that row and are not equivalent.

quiz.q: Use De Morgan and other laws to simplify ¬(p∨(q∧r)).

quiz.a: (p∧q)∨(p∧¬q) ≡ p∧(q∨¬q) by distributivity. Then q∨¬q ≡ T by the negation law. Then p∧T ≡ p by identity. The answer is p.

quiz.q: A student says: If a number is divisible by 4, it is even. Therefore, if a number is even, it is divisible by 4. Identify the logical error.
quiz.a: The student has used the converse q→p of the true implication p→q. The converse is not equivalent to the original. For example, 6 is even but not divisible by 4.

quiz.q: Show that the inverse of p→q is equivalent to the converse of p→q.
quiz.a: Inverse: ¬p→¬q ≡ p∨¬q using implication. Converse: q→p ≡ ¬q∨p using implication. The two results p∨¬q and ¬q∨p are the same by commutativity. So the inverse and converse are equivalent to each other.

quiz.q: Write the contrapositive of: If the Chennai power cut lasts more than 2 hours, the backup generator starts.
quiz.a: If the backup generator does not start, the Chennai power cut did not last more than 2 hours.

beyond: Not for the exam. Logical equivalences are the rewrite rules inside SAT solvers and hardware logic minimisers. Formal verification tools such as Coq and Lean use contrapositive and De Morgan reasoning constantly. Query optimisers in databases use equivalences to rewrite SQL conditions into cheaper forms. Search for propositional equivalence SAT solver, contrapositive proof in mathematics, and De Morgan laws in programming to go further.
